unit.title: Use and maintain graduated measuring devices

summary: This unit teaches you to choose, use and look after graduated measuring devices: steel rules, tape measures, vernier calipers, micrometers, protractors and gauges. You will learn to read each scale accurately, avoid the usual measuring errors, record readings and judge them against a tolerance, and keep devices clean, calibrated and safely stored. The unit is shared by several Level 2 programmes, so the examples come from welding and fabrication and from electrical installation.

blocks.p: A **graduated measuring device** is a measuring tool marked with a scale of equal divisions, such as millimetres or degrees. Steel rules, tape measures, vernier calipers, micrometers and protractors are all graduated devices. This unit teaches you to choose the right device for a job, read it accurately, record what you find, and keep the device in good order so that it stays accurate.

Every trade depends on measurement. A fabricator who cuts a gate rail 5 mm short wastes steel and time. An electrician who measures a cable run wrongly ends up with a joint where none should be, or with metres of costly cable thrown away. Accurate measurement saves material, time and money, makes the work fit and safe, and lets it pass inspection the first time.

**Who it is for:** Level 2 trainees in welding and fabrication, electrical installation and other engineering trades at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres. The unit is shared by several programmes, so the examples come from more than one trade.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Pick a device that can reach the size and that reads finer than the tolerance on the drawing.
Look for damage, check that moving parts run smoothly, check the zero, and check the calibration label.
Measure lengths, widths and positions from a datum, with the rule or tape held straight and square.
Take outside, inside and depth measurements and read the vernier scale to 0.02 mm.
Measure thicknesses and diameters to 0.01 mm, using the ratchet for even pressure.
Use protractors, squares, feeler gauges and dial indicators correctly.
Control parallax, dirt, pressure, heat and slanting; write readings down with their units; judge them against the tolerance.
Clean, oil and store devices; have them checked against standards; label and report any that are faulty or out of date.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on choosing devices, reading scales, sources of error, units, tolerances, care and calibration.
A **written paper** with short answers (part names, unit changes, scale readings) and longer answers in full sentences, showing any working.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: measuring a set of workshop parts with the right devices and checking them against tolerances; and checking, cleaning, testing and storing a set of devices, with a check register. The assessor watches how you work, not only your answers.

blocks.note: Practise reading vernier and micrometer scales until you are quick and sure. Readings come up in every part of the assessment, and a missed half-millimetre line on a micrometer is the most common mistake.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Units, accuracy and choosing a device

blocks.p: Engineering work uses the metric (SI) system. The base unit of length is the **metre (m)**. Engineering drawings give sizes in **millimetres (mm)**, usually with a note such as ALL DIMENSIONS IN MM, so the unit is not written after every number.

head: Unit
Symbol
Equal to
Typical use
rows: Bar and pipe lengths, cable runs, room sizes
Printed on some tapes; rarely used on engineering drawings
One thousandth of a metre (0.001 m)
Almost every size on a drawing
Micrometer readings: sheet, wire and pin sizes

ul: Metres to millimetres: multiply by 1 000. For example, 4.25 m = 4 250 mm.
Millimetres to metres: divide by 1 000. For example, 860 mm = 0.86 m.
Inches to millimetres: multiply by **25.4** (an exact figure). For example, 2 in = 50.8 mm, and 1 foot (12 in) = 304.8 mm.
Millimetres to inches: divide by 25.4. For example, 100 mm is about 3.94 in.

blocks.note: Metric units are the standard for engineering work in Jamaica, but feet and inches are still common in hardware stores, on older drawings and for some fittings: you will hear of ½-inch conduit, steel in 20-foot lengths (about 6 m) and 4 ft × 8 ft sheets (about 1 220 mm × 2 440 mm). Change everything to millimetres before you start, and always write down the unit you used.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The smallest to the largest size the device can measure
A 0–25 mm micrometer cannot measure a 30 mm bar.
The smallest change in size the device can show: its smallest division or step
Steel rule 0.5 mm or 1 mm; vernier caliper 0.02 mm; micrometer 0.01 mm
How close the reading is to the true size
A dropped caliper still has 0.02 mm divisions, but its bent jaws may give a reading that is well out.
Getting the same reading each time the same thing is measured the same way
Two trainees who measure the same bar correctly should agree.

blocks.note: Fine divisions do not make a reading right. A device is only as good as its condition, its zero and the way you use it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Choose a device that can **reach the size** and that **reads clearly finer than the tolerance**: the smaller the tolerance, the finer the device you need. Then think about the shape of the feature: is it a length, an outside size, an inside size, a depth or an angle?

head: Device
Typical range
Reads to
Use it for
rows: Long lengths: bars, frames, cable and conduit runs, room sizes
Shorter lengths, marking cut lines, setting gaps; its edge also checks flatness
Vernier caliper (or dial or digital caliper)
Outside, inside and depth sizes: bar, pipe and conduit diameters, plate thickness, hole depth
25 mm steps: 0–25, 25–50, 50–75 mm and so on
The most exact work: sheet, wire and conductor thickness, pin and shaft sizes
Angles of bevels, mitres and bends
The thickness marked on each blade
Very small movements: wobble (run-out), flatness, alignment

blocks.p: A **tolerance** is how much a size may vary from the drawing size and still be accepted. The largest and smallest sizes allowed are the **limits**. The difference between the limits is the total tolerance.
When a size has no tolerance beside it, the drawing's **general tolerance** applies. It is usually printed in or near the title block, for example: UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED, TOLERANCE ± 0.5.

blocks.note: Work out both limits and write them down before you start measuring. Then each reading becomes a quick yes or no.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Reading a metric rule or tape

ul: The long numbered marks are every **10 mm**. On some tapes the numbers are centimetres (1, 2, 3 ...), on others millimetres (10, 20, 30 ...). Check which before you read.
The medium mark halfway between two numbers is the 5 mm mark.
The short marks are single millimetres. Many steel rules also have a half-millimetre (0.5 mm) scale along one edge.
Tapes mark each metre clearly. Read the metres, then the millimetres: 2 m and 375 mm is written 2 375 mm.

blocks.p: **Worked example:** on a tape numbered in centimetres, the end of a bar falls three short marks after the number 47. That is 470 mm + 3 mm = **473 mm**.

ul: Stand the rule **on its edge**, so that the marks touch the work. Laid flat, the thickness of the rule lifts the marks off the work and makes parallax error more likely.
Hold the rule square to the edge you measure from. A rule at a slant reads too long.

The end of a rule wears and gets knocked round. For an exact reading, line the work up with the 10 mm mark instead and take 10 mm off the reading, or butt the end of the rule against a square held on the edge of the work.
Read with your eye straight over the mark.
Mark with a fine scribed line or a sharp pencil. A thick chalk or soapstone line can hide a millimetre or two.
Never use a rule as a screwdriver, a scraper or a lever: a nicked edge no longer gives a true line.

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: The steel strip printed with the scale; curved across its width so that it stands out straight
Grips the end or edge of the work; slides a little, by its own thickness
Rivets firm; the hook moves only its small built-in amount
Holds the blade; many show their own length on the back, for inside measurements
Holds the blade out at a length

blocks.p: The hook slides **out** by its own thickness when you hook it over an edge and pull, and slides **in** by its thickness when you push it against a surface. Either way, the reading starts from the true zero. A hook that is bent, or whose rivets have been squeezed tight, makes every reading wrong by a millimetre or more.

ul: **Outside measurements:** hook over the end, pull the blade straight and taut, keep it flat and square to the edge, and read with your eye straight over the mark.
**Inside measurements:** push the hook against one face. If the case goes into the corner, add the case length printed on it.

**Long lengths:** keep the blade straight and taut, with a helper at the far end if needed. A tape that sags or wanders off line follows a longer path than the true distance, so it reads **too long**.
**Exact work with a doubtful hook:** measure from the 100 mm mark and take 100 mm off the reading. Tradesmen call this "burning" 100 mm. Report the damaged tape as well.
Let the blade wind back slowly. A blade that snaps back bends the hook and loosens its rivets, and its edge can cut your fingers.
Wipe the blade dry before it goes back into the case, especially after rain or sweat.

blocks.p: Mark all the positions along a bar, a wall or a board from **one starting point**, the **datum**: a squared end, an edge or a centre line. If you measure each mark from the one before (chain measuring), every small error is added to the next, and by the tenth mark you may be several millimetres out.
**Example:** holes every 300 mm along a 3 m bar. Hook the tape on the squared end once and mark 300, 600, 900 ... 2 700 mm, rather than measuring 300 mm from each mark to the next.

A rectangular frame is square when its **two diagonals are equal**. Measure corner to corner both ways with the tape. If one diagonal is longer, push the two long corners towards each other until the diagonals match, then tack or fix the frame. For example, both diagonals of a 1 800 mm × 1 200 mm frame should be about 2 163 mm.

blocks.note: Measure twice, cut once. Before you cut or drill, read the size on the drawing again, measure again from the datum, and check that the cut will be on the waste side of the line.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Part
What it does
rows: The long fixed bar that carries the main scale in millimetres
Part of the beam; one side of every measurement
Slides along the beam and carries the vernier scale
Measure outside sizes: thickness, width, bar or conduit diameter
Measure inside sizes: the bore of a pipe, the width of a slot
Slides out of the end of the beam to measure the depth of a hole or a step
Locks the sliding jaw so the reading cannot change while you take the caliper off the work
The short scale on the sliding jaw that gives the fine reading

blocks.p: On a 0.02 mm caliper the vernier scale has **50 divisions** that together cover 49 mm of the main scale, so each vernier division is 0.98 mm: 0.02 mm shorter than a main-scale millimetre. When the jaws open by 0.02 mm, the first vernier line moves into line with a main-scale line; at 0.04 mm the second line lines up; and so on. The vernier line that lines up tells you how many 0.02 mm steps to add to the main-scale reading.
The vernier is usually numbered 0, 1, 2 ... 10. Each number stands for **0.1 mm** (five lines of 0.02 mm), so the line marked 4 is worth 0.40 mm.

flow: Read the main scale at the last whole millimetre **before** the vernier zero (for example 41 mm)
Find the one vernier line that lines up exactly with a line on the main scale (any main-scale line)
Work out its value: the number before it × 0.1 mm, plus 0.02 mm for each line after that number (two lines after the 4: 0.40 + 0.04 = 0.44 mm)
Add the two parts: 41 + 0.44 = 41.44 mm
Write the reading down at once, with its unit

head: Main scale (before the vernier zero)
Vernier line that lines up
Reading
rows: The 0 line, exactly on the 26 mm mark

blocks.note: Not every caliper reads to 0.02 mm. A 0.05 mm caliper has 20 vernier divisions, each worth 0.05 mm. The value is printed on the sliding jaw (for example 0.02 mm or 1/50 mm): check it before you read.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: A **dial caliper** shows the fraction of a millimetre on a dial. Read the whole millimetres on the beam, then add the dial reading.

A **digital caliper** shows the reading on a display, usually to 0.01 mm. Close the jaws and press ZERO before you measure, check that it is set to mm and not inches, and change a weak battery (the display flickers or the numbers jump).
A display that shows 0.01 mm does not make the caliper more accurate than a good vernier. Most calipers are only accurate to about 0.02–0.03 mm, whatever the display shows.

head: Measurement
How to do it
Watch for
rows: Open the jaws wider than the part, put the part well into the jaws close to the beam, and close the sliding jaw gently with the thumb wheel.
Measuring on the thin tips of the jaws
Jaws tilted on the work: both give a wrong size
Put the small inside jaws into the hole and open them gently until they touch both sides.
In a round hole, rock the caliper slightly: the true diameter is the **largest** reading you can find
In a slot, keep the jaws square to its sides
Rest the end of the beam flat on the top face and push the depth rod down until it touches the bottom.
The end of the beam must sit square, not tilted
Clear swarf and dirt out of the bottom first

ul: Clean the jaws and the part. Remove burrs, paint, slag and spatter where you measure.
Check the zero: close the jaws gently. The vernier zero should line up with the main-scale zero (or the display should read 0.00).
Use **light, even pressure**. Squeezing springs the jaws and squashes soft materials such as cable sheaths and plastic conduit.
Lock the sliding jaw before you take the caliper off the work if you cannot read it in place.
Measure in two or three places: round bar can be oval, and plate can vary in thickness.

blocks.note: A fitting's trade size is a name, not a measurement. Conduit sold as ¾-inch, for example, measures about 26.7 mm across the outside when it is the common PVC type. When you order glands, fittings or clips, measure the real outside diameter with a caliper and check it against the maker's table.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Part
What it does
rows: The U-shaped body that holds the anvil and spindle in line; many have an insulating pad to hold it by
The fixed measuring face; the work rests against it
The moving measuring face; it screws towards the anvil to close on the work
Locks the spindle so that the reading holds
The fixed scale: whole millimetres on one side of the datum line, half millimetres on the other
Turns the spindle; its bevelled edge carries 50 divisions
Slips once the faces touch the work, so every measurement is made with the same light pressure

blocks.p: The spindle is a fine screw with a **pitch of 0.5 mm**: one full turn of the thimble moves it 0.5 mm. The thimble has **50 divisions**, so each division is 0.5 ÷ 50 = **0.01 mm**. Two full turns move the spindle 1 mm.

flow: Read the whole millimetres showing on the sleeve (for example 5 mm)
Look for a half-millimetre line showing after the last whole millimetre; if one is showing, add 0.5 mm
Read the thimble division that lines up with the datum line on the sleeve (for example 42, which is 0.42 mm)
Add the parts: 5 + 0.5 + 0.42 = 5.92 mm
Write the reading down at once, with its unit

blocks.note: The half-millimetre line is the part of a micrometer reading most often missed. A thimble reading near 0 means a line has only just appeared on the sleeve; a reading near 49 means the next line is about to appear but has not. Look closely, and if a reading seems 0.5 mm out from what you expected, read it again.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Each micrometer covers only 25 mm: 0–25 mm, 25–50 mm, 50–75 mm and so on. On a 25–50 mm micrometer, add 25 mm to the sleeve reading unless the sleeve is marked from 25. Micrometers larger than 0–25 mm come with a **setting standard** (setting rod) of exact length, used to check the zero.

flow: Choose the micrometer whose range covers the size
Clean the anvil, the spindle face and the work with a clean, soft cloth
Check the zero: close the faces gently with the ratchet (or on the setting standard for a larger micrometer)
Hold the micrometer by the frame or its insulating pad, for as short a time as you can
Open it a little wider than the work and place the work square between the anvil and the spindle
Turn the ratchet until it clicks two or three times; never force the thimble
Lock the spindle if you must take the micrometer off to read it; read and record
Measure in more than one place: a round part across two diameters at 90° to each other, to find out whether it is oval

blocks.p: If a micrometer does not read 0.00 with its faces closed, it has a **zero error**. Report it, and have it adjusted by someone trained to do it (most micrometers come with a small C-spanner for this). Until then you can allow for the error:

ul: Closed reading **+0.02 mm** (the thimble's 2 is on the datum line): every reading is 0.02 mm too big, so **take 0.02 mm off**.
Closed reading **−0.02 mm** (the thimble's zero has gone past the line and its 48 is on the datum line): every reading is 0.02 mm too small, so **add 0.02 mm**.

blocks.p: A digital micrometer shows the reading on a display, often to 0.001 mm. Close the faces with the ratchet and set the zero before you measure, and check the battery. Cleanliness, light pressure and heat matter just as much as with a plain micrometer.

head: Trade
Typical micrometer jobs
rows: Sheet thickness (for example 1.2 mm or 1.6 mm)
Electrode core wire or filler rod diameter (for example 3.2 mm or 2.4 mm)
Pins and bushes for hinges and gates
Conductor diameter, to tell one size from another: a 12 AWG solid copper conductor is about 2.05 mm across, a 14 AWG about 1.63 mm, and a 2.5 mm² solid conductor about 1.78 mm
Thickness of busbar or a metal plate to be drilled

blocks.p: Angles are measured in **degrees (°)**. A full turn is 360° and a right angle is 90°. For very exact work a degree is split into 60 minutes (60′).

head: Device
Reads to
Used for
rows: Marking and checking angles on drawings, sheet and plate
Protractor head of a combination set
Angles on bar and plate; many have a spirit level built in
Bevel protractor with vernier (universal bevel protractor)
Exact angles on prepared or machined parts
The angles and sizes marked on it
Checking a weld bevel (for example 30° or 37.5°) and fillet weld sizes
Copying an angle from one place to another; set it from a protractor

ul: Put the centre mark of the protractor exactly on the corner (vertex) of the angle, with the base line along one side.
Most protractors have **two scales** running in opposite directions. Read the scale that starts at **0 on the side you lined the base up with**. Read on the wrong scale, a 30° angle shows as 150°.
Ask which edge the angle is measured from. A weld bevel of 30° is 30° from the square edge of the plate; measured from the plate's face, the same bevel shows 60°.

An **engineer's try square**, or the square head of a combination set, checks that two faces meet at **90°**. Hold the stock firmly against one face, slide the blade down onto the other and look for light between the blade and the work. No light means square.
The square head of a combination set also has a **45° face** for marking and checking mitres.
A **centre head** on a combination set finds the centre of the end of a round bar.

To test a square, draw a line along its blade with the stock against a straight edge, turn the square over and draw again from the same point. If the two lines do not match, the square is out: report it.

blocks.h: Gauges for gaps and small movements

head: Gauge
What it is
How to use it
rows: A set of thin steel blades, each marked with its thickness, often from about 0.05 mm to 1 mm
Slide blades into the gap until one goes in with a slight drag
Put blades together for bigger gaps: 0.40 + 0.25 = 0.65 mm
Never force or bend a blade; wipe and lightly oil the set after use
A clock-faced instrument: moving its plunger turns the needle, often 0.01 mm per division and 1 mm per turn, with a small counter for whole turns
Fix it on a magnetic or clamp stand
Press the plunger in a little, then turn the bezel to set zero
Move the work and read the change; used for the wobble (run-out) of shafts and pulleys, and for alignment
Blades cut to inside and outside curves of marked radius
Hold against a curve until one fits with no light showing
A gauge cut to measure the leg length or throat of a fillet weld
Hold it against the plates and the cleaned weld
Blades cut with thread shapes of marked pitch
Try blades in the thread until one fits exactly

blocks.p: **Reading run-out:** if a dial indicator set to zero on a turning shaft swings from −0.03 mm to +0.05 mm, the total run-out is 0.03 + 0.05 = **0.08 mm**.

blocks.note: A spirit level is not a graduated measuring device, but you will use it alongside them: electricians to set boards, trunking and conduit level and plumb, fabricators to set frames and posts. To check a level, read it on a surface, turn it end for end in exactly the same place and read again: the bubble should sit in the same place both times.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Source of error
What happens
How to avoid it
rows: Looking at the scale from an angle makes the mark seem to line up with the wrong line
Put your eye straight in line with the mark; stand a rule on its edge
Dirt, burrs, paint, slag or spatter
They sit between the device and the work, so the reading is too big
Clean the work and the device's faces; file off burrs; measure on clean metal
Caliper jaws spring, thin sheet bends, soft materials such as insulation and plastic squash
Light, even pressure; the ratchet on a micrometer
Device not square; tape slanting or sagging
The device measures a longer path than the true distance, so it reads too long
Hold rules and tapes straight, taut and square to the edge; support long tapes
Worn or damaged device; wrong zero
Readings are out, by the same amount each time or by different amounts
Check the condition and the zero before use; use an in-date device; report faults
Metal grows as it warms: steel by about 0.012 mm per metre for each °C
Measure parts after they have cooled; do not hold precision tools longer than needed; keep them out of the sun
A 6 read as 9, a half-millimetre line missed, the wrong unit, two figures swapped
Read twice, write the reading down at once with its unit, and have someone check it
Small errors add up when each mark is measured from the one before
Measure every mark from one datum

blocks.p: Precision measuring devices are made to read correctly at **20 °C**. Steel lying in the Jamaican sun gets far hotter than that, and a part that has just been welded, cut or ground is hotter still. A 1 m steel bar that is 50 °C hotter than when it was measured is about **0.6 mm** longer (1 000 mm × 0.012 mm × 50 ÷ 1 000). That hardly matters on a gate post with a ±2 mm tolerance, but it matters a great deal on a part checked to ±0.1 mm.

ul: Measure finished parts when they have cooled to the temperature of the workshop.

A steel tape and a steel bar lying in the same sun grow by about the same amount, so the error mostly cancels. The trouble comes from a hot part measured with a cool precision tool, or a tool warmed in your hand.
Keep precision tools in their cases, out of the sun and away from hot work.

blocks.p: Write each reading down **as soon as you take it**, with its unit. A reading carried in your head is soon forgotten or mixed up with the next one. A simple measuring sheet keeps everything together:

ul: Note the date, your name or initials, and the device's ID number if it has one.
If a second person checks a reading and gets a different answer, measure again together until you agree. Never just choose the reading that suits you.
A part outside its limits is labelled, set aside and reported. It is not hidden, and it is not forced to fit.

blocks.note: Measure twice. A second reading, by you or better by another person, catches most mistakes before material is cut, a hole is drilled or a fitting is fixed.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Wipe every device clean after use with a soft, clean cloth. Dust, filings, oil, sweat and fingerprints cause rust and wear.
Give bare steel devices a **thin film of light oil** or rust preventive, and wipe off the excess.
Store each device in its own case or a padded drawer, away from heavy tools.
Leave a **small gap** between the faces of a micrometer or caliper when you store it, with the lock off.
Never use a measuring device as a hammer, clamp, spanner, scraper, screwdriver or scriber, and never force a jaw, a spindle or a thimble.
Never measure work that is moving, or work that is still hot.
Keep devices on a cloth on the bench, back from the edge, where they cannot roll off or be knocked down.
Keep devices away from grinding, welding and cutting: sparks and spatter pit the faces and scales.
Let a tape wind back slowly, and dry it if it is wet.

blocks.note: Jamaica's warm, humid air, and the salt air near the coast, make bare steel rust quickly. A rule or a caliper left out on a bench can show rust spots within days, and rust soon eats into the scale. Clean, oil and case your devices every time, and keep them in a dry, closed cupboard: not in a damp corner of the store room, and not on a window sill in the sun.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: **Calibration** means checking a device against a **standard of known size**, recording how far it is out, and then adjusting it, noting its error, or taking it out of use. Devices wear, get knocked and drift, so they are checked at set times (often once a year, or more often for devices in heavy use) and whenever one may have been damaged.

head: Standard
What it is
Used to check
rows: Hardened steel or ceramic blocks made to an exact size
Vernier calipers, micrometers and dial indicators
A rod of exact length supplied with micrometers above 25 mm
The zero of a 25–50 mm or larger micrometer
A steel rule of known accuracy
A good rule kept for checking only
Tape measures: the hook and the first few hundred millimetres
A square of known accuracy kept for checking only

blocks.p: Calibrated devices usually carry a **label** showing the device's ID number, the date it was checked, the date the next check is due and who checked it. The results go in a **register** (a device check record), so anyone can see each device's history.

flow: Inspect the device for damage and wear; check that moving parts run smoothly
Clean the measuring faces and the standard
Check the zero
Measure the standard in the normal way (for example a 25.00 mm gauge block)
Record the reading and the difference (for example 25.02 mm: +0.02 mm)
Compare the difference with the limit the Centre allows: pass, adjust (only if you are trained), or fail
Label the device (in date, or FAULTY – DO NOT USE) and fill in the register

ul: To check a tape, lay it against a good steel rule and compare the hook (both pulled and pushed) and the first 300 mm of marks.
Handle gauge blocks as little as possible, so that your hand does not warm them. Wipe them clean, never drop them or let them roll, and put each one back in its place in the box.
Let the device and the standard sit together for a while first, so that they are at the same temperature.

flow: Stop using it
Label it, for example FAULTY – DO NOT USE, with the date and the fault
Keep it apart from the good devices
Report it to your instructor, supervisor or storekeeper
Carry on with another device that is in date and in good order

blocks.p: Do not try to straighten, file or adjust a precision device yourself unless you are trained and allowed to. A home repair usually makes it worse, and it hides the fault from the next user.

blocks.note: Workplaces that need traceable measurements send their master standards and gauge blocks to a calibration laboratory. In Jamaica, the Bureau of Standards Jamaica offers calibration services; your Centre will have its own system and its own forms for the in-house checks you will do.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what a graduated measuring device is and name the common ones.
I can change metres to millimetres and back, and inches to millimetres.
I can explain range, resolution, accuracy and tolerance, and work out the limits of a toleranced size.
I can choose a device that can reach the size and reads finer than the tolerance.
I can check a device before use: condition, moving parts, zero and calibration label.
I can measure with a steel rule and a tape measure, outside and inside, from a datum.
I can check a frame for square by its diagonals.
I can name the parts of a vernier caliper and read it to 0.02 mm.
I can take outside, inside and depth measurements with a caliper using light pressure.
I can name the parts of a micrometer and read it to 0.01 mm, including the half-millimetre line.
I can check a micrometer's zero and allow for a zero error.
I can measure angles with a protractor, reading the right scale, and check squareness with a square.
I can use feeler gauges and read a dial indicator.
I can name the main sources of measuring error and say how to avoid each one.
I can record readings clearly, with units, and decide whether each one is within tolerance.
I can clean, oil and store measuring devices so that they stay accurate.
I can check a device against a standard, record the result, and label and report a faulty device.

terms: Accuracy
How close a reading is to the true size
Anvil
The fixed measuring face of a micrometer
Beam
The long fixed bar of a vernier caliper that carries the main scale
Calibration
Checking a device against a standard of known size, then adjusting it, recording its error or taking it out of use
Datum
The line, edge or point that measurements are taken from
Depth rod
The thin rod that slides out of the end of a caliper to measure depths
Dial indicator
A clock-faced instrument that measures very small movements
Feeler gauge
A set of thin steel blades of marked thickness, for measuring small gaps
Gauge block
A hardened block of exact size used to check measuring devices; also called a slip gauge
Graduated
Marked with a scale of equal divisions
Limits
The largest and smallest sizes a tolerance allows
Locking screw
The screw that holds a caliper's sliding jaw so the reading cannot change
Main scale
The millimetre scale on a caliper's beam
Millimetre (mm)
One thousandth of a metre; the unit of size on engineering drawings
Parallax error
A wrong reading caused by looking at a scale from an angle
Range
The smallest to the largest size a device can measure
Ratchet
The part of a micrometer that slips at the right pressure, so every measurement uses the same light force
Resolution
The smallest change in size a device can show
Run-out
The wobble of a turning part, measured with a dial indicator
Setting standard
A rod of exact length used to check the zero of a larger micrometer
Sleeve
The fixed scale of a micrometer, in whole and half millimetres
Spindle
The moving measuring face of a micrometer
Thimble
The part of a micrometer you turn; it carries a scale of 50 divisions
Tolerance
How much a size may vary from the drawing size and still be accepted
Vernier scale
The short scale on a caliper's sliding jaw that gives the fine reading
Zero error
A reading other than zero when a device is closed; it must be allowed for or corrected

c1.title: Gate frames in Old Harbour
c1.text: Jermaine, a welding trainee on work experience, is cutting 25 mm square tube for two gate frames at a small fabrication shop in Old Harbour, St Catherine. Each frame is 1 800 mm wide and 1 200 mm high, and every rail must be within ±2 mm. The tube comes in 6 m lengths and is stored on a rack in full sun. The only tape in the shop has a bent end hook.

c2.title: Conduit and cable at a health centre in Santa Cruz
c2.text: Shanice, an electrical installation trainee, is helping to rewire a health centre in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. Her supervisor has given her a 0.02 mm vernier caliper to check the conduit, cables and fittings before they are fixed. The PVC conduit is sold as ¾-inch, and the supervisor wants the outside diameter of each cable so that the right cable glands can be ordered.

c3.title: Pins and sheet for boat fittings in Port Maria
c3.text: Odane works in a small engineering shop in Port Maria, St Mary, that makes stainless-steel and mild-steel fittings for fishing boats. He uses a 0–25 mm outside micrometer to check sheet thickness and the diameter of hinge pins. Before he starts, he cleans the faces and closes them with the ratchet: the thimble reads 3 divisions past zero (+0.03 mm). There is no one in the shop trained to adjust it today.

c4.title: The device check in Morant Bay
c4.text: Before a new term at a training centre in Morant Bay, St Thomas, Kimberley and two classmates check the workshop's measuring devices. The store room is near the sea, and its window has been left open for weeks. They find a 300 mm steel rule with rust spots, a vernier caliper that reads 25.06 mm on a 25.00 mm gauge block (the Centre allows ±0.02 mm), and a tape measure with a sharp kink in the blade at 1.4 m.

c5.title: Bevelled plates in Bog Walk
c5.text: At a steel shop in Bog Walk, St Catherine, Tavia is checking plates that have been bevelled for single-V butt joints. The drawing asks for a 30° bevel (±2°) and a 2 mm root face (±0.5 mm). She has a half-circle protractor with two scales, a combination set, a steel rule and a 0.02 mm vernier caliper.

questions.q: With the bent hook, how can Jermaine still take true lengths from that tape while a new one is ordered?
o: Hook it over the end as usual, because a bent hook only spoils inside readings
Push the hook against the end of the tube instead of hooking it over
Measure from the 100 mm mark and take 100 mm off every reading
Add the thickness of the hook to every reading that he takes
questions.why: Starting from the 100 mm mark ("burning" 100 mm) takes the damaged hook out of the measurement altogether. A bent hook no longer moves by exactly its own thickness, so readings taken from it are wrong both ways.

questions.q: After tacking the first frame, Jermaine measures its diagonals: 2 168 mm one way and 2 159 mm the other. What does this tell him?
o: It is out of square: ease the long corners together until they match
The frame is square, since diagonals of a rectangle are never exactly the same
One of the rails is 9 mm too long and must be cut down before he welds
The tape has stretched over the longer distance and should be replaced
questions.why: A rectangle is square only when its two diagonals are equal; for 1 800 mm × 1 200 mm both should be about 2 163 mm. A 9 mm difference means the frame has racked, so it is pushed square while the tacks are still small.

questions.q: The tube and the tape have both been lying in the sun at about 50 °C. Should this worry Jermaine for these ±2 mm rails?
o: Yes: he must wait until the steel is cool before he measures or cuts
No: the growth is well under a millimetre, far inside the ±2 mm
Yes: the sun stretches a tape's blade by several millimetres
No: steel does not grow at the temperatures found in Jamaica
questions.why: Steel grows about 0.012 mm per metre for each °C: a 1 800 mm rail 30 °C above 20 °C grows only about 0.65 mm, and a steel tape in the same sun grows almost as much. Heat matters for fine tolerances, not for a ±2 mm gate rail.

questions.q: One finished rail measures 1 797 mm. What should happen to it?
o: Use it, as 3 mm will not show on a finished gate
Measure it again from the other end until it reads 1 798 mm
Grind the matching rail 3 mm shorter so that the two agree
Label it, set it aside and tell the supervisor it is short
questions.why: The limits are 1 798–1 802 mm, so 1 797 mm is outside the tolerance and cannot be stretched. A part outside its limits is labelled, set aside and reported, never hidden or measured again until it gives the answer you want.

questions.q: Shanice measures the ¾-inch conduit and reads 26.68 mm across the outside. Why is it not 19 mm?
o: Her caliper is set to read in inches, not in millimetres
The trade size is a name, not the real outside diameter
She has squeezed the jaws too hard on the soft PVC
The vernier lines up on the wrong side of the zero
questions.why: Conduit and pipe are sold by a trade size that is a name, not a measurement; ¾-inch PVC conduit measures about 26.7 mm outside. That is why fittings and glands are chosen from a real measurement and the maker's table.

questions.q: For one cable, Shanice sees 14 on the beam, and the matching line on the sliding jaw is three after the 6. How should she write the size down?
questions.why: The 6 is worth 0.60 mm and each line after it adds 0.02 mm: 0.60 + 0.06 = 0.66 mm, so the reading is 14 + 0.66 = 14.66 mm. Counting each line as 0.01 mm gives the common wrong answer of 14.63 mm.

questions.q: The cables have soft PVC sheaths. How should Shanice close the caliper on them?
o: Squeeze firmly so the jaws grip the cable and cannot slip
Use the small inside jaws, as they are thinner and sharper
Close the jaws gently until they just touch the sheath
Measure once only, at the cut end, where it is easiest
questions.why: Too much pressure squashes soft materials and springs the jaws, so the reading comes out small. Light, even pressure, measured in two or three places along the cable, gives a true diameter.

questions.q: Shanice measures the bore of a piece of steel conduit with the inside jaws, and the reading changes as she moves the caliper. Which reading is the true bore?
o: The first reading, before the jaws have moved
The smallest reading she can find across it
The average of her first and last readings
The largest reading she can find across it
questions.why: Across a round hole, the jaws read less than the diameter whenever they are off centre or tilted. Rocking the caliper gently and taking the largest reading finds the true diameter.

questions.q: Odane measures a pin and reads 9.47 mm. Allowing for the zero error he found, what is the pin's true size?
questions.why: With the faces closed the micrometer already reads +0.03 mm, so every reading is 0.03 mm too big: 9.47 − 0.03 = 9.44 mm. He should also report the error so the micrometer can be adjusted.

questions.q: Odane reads a sheet as 3.12 mm, but his supervisor reads 3.62 mm on the same micrometer setting. What has Odane most likely missed?
o: The half-millimetre line showing on the sleeve
The zero error on the micrometer's thimble scale
The 25 mm to be added for the range
A thimble division worth 0.05 mm each
questions.why: A difference of exactly 0.5 mm points to the half-millimetre line on the sleeve. A zero error here is only 0.03 mm, and a 0–25 mm micrometer needs no 25 mm added.

questions.q: A pin reads 9.98 mm across one diameter and 9.91 mm across a diameter at 90° to the first, at the same place on the pin. What does this show?
o: The micrometer has a zero error of 0.07 mm
The pin is tapered along its length
The pin is oval, out of round by 0.07 mm
He used too much pressure the second time
questions.why: Two diameters at 90° to each other at the same place should match on a round pin; a difference shows ovality. A taper shows up when readings change along the length, and a zero error would affect both readings equally.

questions.q: Odane now has to check a 32 mm stainless-steel shaft. Which device should he use?
o: The 0–25 mm micrometer, adding 25 mm to its reading
A 25–50 mm micrometer, checked on its setting standard
The 0–25 mm micrometer, opened as far as it will go
A 50–75 mm micrometer, as a larger size is always safer
questions.why: Each micrometer covers only 25 mm, so a 32 mm shaft needs the 25–50 mm size. Its zero is checked on the 25 mm setting standard because its faces cannot be closed together.

questions.q: What should Kimberley's group record and do about the vernier caliper?
o: Record +0.06 mm; label it faulty and report it
Record −0.06 mm; it reads small, so pass it
Record 25.06 mm only; errors under 0.1 mm do not matter
Close the jaws harder until they read 25.00, then pass it
questions.why: The caliper reads 0.06 mm more than the block, an error of +0.06 mm, three times what the Centre allows. It fails: it is labelled, kept apart and reported, and the reading and the difference go in the register.

questions.q: Which change would do most to stop the store room's devices rusting again?
o: Wash the devices in fresh water each week to get the salt off
Lay the devices on the window sill where the sun can dry them
Shut the window, oil the devices lightly and keep them cased
Wrap each device in a damp cloth to keep the dust off it
questions.why: Salt, damp air and moisture cause rust; a thin film of oil and a closed, dry place keep it away. Water and sunlight on a window sill make rust and heat damage worse, not better.

questions.q: What should be done with the tape measure that has a kink at 1.4 m?
o: Label it faulty and report it so that it can be replaced
Straighten the kink with pliers and put it back in the store
Keep it for measuring lengths of less than 1.4 m only
Hammer the kink flat on the anvil, then check it on a rule
questions.why: A kinked blade no longer lies straight, will not stand out properly and soon tears at the kink. Home repairs hide the fault, so the tape is labelled, taken out of use and reported.

questions.q: How should the group handle the gauge blocks during the check?
o: Hold them in the hand while the devices are checked, so they warm up
Clean them with emery cloth so that the faces are bright and smooth
Leave them out on the bench afterwards so the next group can use them
Touch them as little as possible and return them clean to their box
questions.why: Gauge blocks are the standard every device is judged by, so they must not be warmed, scratched or dropped. Hand heat makes them grow, and an abrasive spoils their exact faces.

questions.q: Where the bevel crosses Tavia's protractor, she sees two numbers: 30 and 150. How does she know which one to read?
o: Always take the smaller of the two numbers shown
Read the outer scale, as the inner one is for drawings
Read the scale that starts at 0 on her base line
Read whichever scale is printed larger and clearer
questions.why: The two scales run in opposite directions, and only the one starting at zero on the side the base is lined up with gives the true angle. "Always the smaller number" works only by luck.

questions.q: Which of Tavia's devices is best for checking the 2 mm (±0.5 mm) root face?
o: The 0.02 mm vernier caliper
The steel rule's half-millimetre scale
The protractor's straight edge
The tape measure's first 10 mm
questions.why: The total tolerance is only 1 mm, so the device must read well finer than that; a rule's 0.5 mm divisions are as coarse as the tolerance itself, so a 2.4 mm root face and a 2.6 mm one look the same on it. The caliper reads to 0.02 mm.

questions.q: An old drawing for a pump bracket gives a hole spacing of 3¼ inches. What is that in millimetres?
questions.why: One inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so 3.25 × 25.4 = 82.55 mm. Using 25 instead of 25.4 gives 81.25 mm, and using 2.54 (centimetres) gives a figure ten times too small.

questions.q: Chevaughn sets a dial indicator to zero on a motor shaft and turns the shaft slowly. The needle swings between −0.04 mm and +0.03 mm. What is the total run-out?
questions.why: Run-out is the full swing of the needle from its lowest to its highest reading: 0.04 + 0.03 = 0.07 mm. Taking only one side, or the difference between the two numbers, gives too small an answer.
